question: What is the principal layout difference between the pathway grade crossing and the sidewalk grade crossing in Figure 8E-1?
model_answer: Direct Answer: The principal layout difference is the right-of-way in which the crossing lies. In Figure 8E-1, the pathway grade crossing (drawing A) sits in its own independent "Pathway right-of-way," separated from any roadway, while the sidewalk grade crossing (drawing B) runs immediately alongside the roadway within the "Highway right-of-way." Because the sidewalk is close to the roadway's traveled way, the roadway grade crossing's traffic control devices can influence or warn sidewalk users, whereas they cannot adequately do so for pathway users. This distinction is explanatory (Support), not a normative requirement. Standards (mandatory): - Although not the layout difference itself, both crossing types share this requirement: "Detectable warnings (see Chapter 3C) shall be used at pathway grade crossings where pedestrian travel is permitted and at sidewalk grade crossings and shall extend across the full width of the pathway or sidewalk." Figure 8E-1 shows detectable warnings on both approaches in both drawings. Support (informational): - A pathway is frequently placed in its own right-of-way on an alignment independent of any roadway; if built parallel to a roadway, it is physically separated by an open space or barrier such that the roadway grade crossing's traffic control devices do not exert an influence over or provide adequate warning to pathway users. - A sidewalk runs parallel to a roadway within the highway right-of-way and is close enough to the edge of the roadway's traveled way that the roadway grade crossing's traffic control devices can frequently exert an influence over or provide adequate warning to sidewalk users. - Pathways are typically used by both pedestrians and bicyclists, whereas sidewalks are typically used only by pedestrians. Visual evidence: - [Image 1] Figure 8E-1 shows drawing A with a standalone pathway crossing the tracks within its own "Pathway right-of-way," and drawing B with a sidewalk crossing the tracks directly adjacent to a roadway, both contained within the "Highway right-of-way." - [Image 2] The full page (p.1035) presents Section 8E.01's explanation alongside Figure 8E-1, confirming that the figure's purpose is to illustrate the pathway-versus-sidewalk right-of-way distinction. - [Image 4] Page 1077 shows Figure 8E-2, in which the sidewalk grade crossing is placed near the roadway crossing with its own flashing-light signals and detectable warnings, consistent with the sidewalk configuration in Figure 8E-1. Citations: - Section 8E.01 Support §4 (p.1035) - Section 8E.04 Standard §7 (p.1038) - Figure 8E-1 (p.1035) - Page 1076 - Page 1077
gold_answer: The pathway crossing is on a separate pathway alignment outside the roadway, whereas the sidewalk crossing is part of the highway corridor alongside the roadway and crosses the tracks with the roadway.
